lesson.title: Sending It Out: How Exocytosis Empties the Cell's Cargo
lesson.summary: Exocytosis is the mirror image of endocytosis, using vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane to release material out of the cell, a mechanism cells rely on for everything from hormone release to neurotransmission.
lesson.body:
If endocytosis is how a cell brings material in by wrapping it in membrane, exocytosis is how a cell sends material back out using the same basic membrane trick run in reverse. A vesicle inside the cytoplasm, often one that budded off from the Golgi apparatus after its contents were packaged and sorted, travels to the plasma membrane, makes contact, and fuses with it. Because both the vesicle membrane and the plasma membrane are phospholipid bilayers, fusion is chemically and structurally possible: the two bilayers merge into one continuous membrane, the vesicle's interior becomes continuous with the extracellular space, and its contents are released outside the cell without ever having to cross an intact membrane barrier.

This fusion event does not happen by chance contact. It is directed by a family of proteins called SNAREs, with one type embedded in the vesicle membrane and a complementary type embedded in the target region of the plasma membrane. When a vesicle approaches the correct docking site, these SNARE proteins bind tightly to each other, zippering together and pulling the two membranes close enough that their lipid bilayers merge. This specificity matters enormously in a cell that may have many different types of vesicles moving toward many different destinations at once, since it helps ensure that vesicles fuse only at the correct location and only when the cell intends them to.

Like endocytosis, exocytosis is an energy-dependent process, both in the sense that vesicles are typically transported to the membrane along the cytoskeleton by ATP-powered motor proteins, and in the sense that the whole secretory pathway leading up to fusion, from protein synthesis through packaging in the Golgi apparatus, consumes cellular energy at multiple steps. This places exocytosis firmly in the same broad category as active transport: a process the cell pays for because it accomplishes something passive membrane properties alone could never achieve, in this case exporting large molecules and bulk material rather than moving individual ions or small solutes.

The physiological importance of exocytosis is difficult to overstate. At a nerve synapse, an arriving electrical signal triggers calcium ions to flow into the nerve terminal, and that calcium influx is the direct trigger for synaptic vesicles loaded with neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents into the synaptic cleft within a fraction of a millisecond, a speed that ordinary vesicle trafficking rarely needs to achieve. Pancreatic beta cells use a slower version of the same mechanism to secrete insulin into the bloodstream in response to rising blood glucose, and glandular cells throughout the digestive tract use it to release digestive enzymes and mucus into the gut lumen.

Exocytosis also plays a quieter but equally important structural role: every time a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, it adds its own lipid bilayer to that membrane, which is one of the main ways cells replace and expand their surface membrane over time, including replacing patches of membrane that were lost during endocytosis. Between them, endocytosis and exocytosis form a continuous cycle of membrane retrieval and delivery, letting a cell's plasma membrane act as a dynamic, constantly renewed boundary rather than a fixed, unchanging wall.
